lead: A polygon is clipped by keeping only the part inside the rectangular window. Clipping its edges one by one fails: the kept pieces are loose segments, not a filled shape. Sutherland–Hodgman clips the polygon as an ordered vertex list against one window boundary at a time, feeding each output list to the next boundary. Four passes produce a smaller polygon. Any renderer that draws shapes partly off-screen needs this.
prereq: You need: 2.6 Line clipping algorithms for the window boundaries and the intersection formula.

sections.h3: Clip the whole list, not single edges

blocks.text: A window is xmin ≤ x ≤ xmax, ymin ≤ y ≤ ymax. Each side is a half-plane. A polygon is a closed chain of vertices v₀, v₁, …, vₙ₋₁ whose inside is filled. Clip each edge separately and the chain breaks into disconnected pieces.

Sutherland–Hodgman processes the whole list. One pass clips the list against one boundary and writes a new ordered list. That output becomes the input of the next boundary. After four passes you have the clipped polygon.
Vertex order must be preserved. The edge from the last vertex back to the first is a real edge; skip it and a corner vanishes. Only a few universities teach this algorithm in depth.
For one boundary, take each edge from previous vertex P to current vertex Q. Each vertex is inside or outside. Four cases apply:

The intersection is where segment PQ crosses the boundary line. For a vertical boundary x = k, t = (k − Px) ÷ (Qx − Px) and the crossing is (k, Py + t (Qy − Py)). For a horizontal boundary y = k, t = (k − Py) ÷ (Qy − Py) and the crossing is (Px + t (Qx − Px), k). If Qx = Px on a vertical boundary, the edge is parallel and no crossing exists.

sections.h3: Pass order, concave polygons and duplicate vertices

blocks.text: Run the passes left, right, bottom, top. Any fixed order works if you keep it. A concave polygon can produce extra edges along the window boundary, connecting separate visible pieces. Those edges have zero width and do not change the filled region; the scan-fill rules in Unit 1 handle them.

Holes and polygons that split into several separate outlines are better clipped with Weiler–Atherton, which walks the subject polygon and the clip polygon together and reconnects them at intersections. After clipping, remove consecutive duplicate vertices: a vertex exactly on the boundary can be output twice, leaving a zero-length edge.

figure.caption: Each pass clips the vertex list against one boundary and hands the new list to the next pass; the final list is the clipped polygon.

spec.title: Sutherland–Hodgman passes
spec.aria: Four clipping passes in a downward chain: left, right, bottom, top, each feeding its output vertex list to the next boundary, ending in the final polygon.

examples.question: Clip the square with vertices (0, 0), (4, 0), (4, 4), (0, 4) in that order against the window x from 1 to 3 and y from 1 to 3 using Sutherland–Hodgman. Give the vertex list after each pass and the final polygon.
steps: Left pass x = 1 (inside x ≥ 1). Edge (0,4)→(0,0): both outside, nothing. Edge (0,0)→(4,0): outside to inside, crossing at x = 1 gives (1,0); output (1,0) and (4,0). Edge (4,0)→(4,4): both inside, output (4,4). Edge (4,4)→(0,4): inside to outside, crossing gives (1,4). List: (1,0), (4,0), (4,4), (1,4).

Right pass x = 3 (inside x ≤ 3). Edge (1,4)→(1,0): both inside, output (1,0). Edge (1,0)→(4,0): inside to outside, crossing at x = 3 gives (3,0). Edge (4,0)→(4,4): both outside, nothing. Edge (4,4)→(1,4): outside to inside, crossing gives (3,4); output (3,4) and (1,4). List: (1,0), (3,0), (3,4), (1,4).

Bottom pass y = 1 (inside y ≥ 1). Edge (1,4)→(1,0): inside to outside, crossing at y = 1 gives (1,1). Edge (1,0)→(3,0): both outside, nothing. Edge (3,0)→(3,4): outside to inside, crossing gives (3,1); output (3,1) and (3,4). Edge (3,4)→(1,4): both inside, output (1,4). List: (1,1), (3,1), (3,4), (1,4).

Top pass y = 3 (inside y ≤ 3). Edge (1,4)→(1,1): outside to inside, crossing at y = 3 gives (1,3); output (1,3) and (1,1). Edge (1,1)→(3,1): both inside, output (3,1). Edge (3,1)→(3,4): inside to outside, crossing gives (3,3). Edge (3,4)→(1,4): both outside, nothing. List: (1,3), (1,1), (3,1), (3,3).
examples.answer: The clipped polygon is the square with vertices (1,1), (3,1), (3,3) and (1,3).

traps: Doing all four boundaries in one pass over the original vertices. Each pass must use the previous pass's output list.
Dropping the closing edge from the last vertex to the first. That edge can contain a corner of the result.
Forgetting to remove duplicate vertices when a vertex lies exactly on the boundary; zero-length edges upset scan filling.
Assuming Sutherland–Hodgman handles holes. It clips a single contour; holes and separate pieces need Weiler–Atherton.

quiz.q: In what order does Sutherland–Hodgman clip a polygon against the four window boundaries?
quiz.a: One boundary at a time, for example left, right, bottom, top; the output list of each pass is the input of the next.

quiz.q: Why can't each polygon edge be clipped independently as a line?
quiz.a: The kept pieces would be disconnected segments and would not form a closed filled polygon; the vertex chain must be rebuilt pass by pass.

quiz.q: Clip the triangle (0,0), (4,0), (2,4) against the left boundary x = 1 only. Give the output vertex list.
Clipping can leave two identical consecutive vertices. Why does this happen, and what should you do?
quiz.a: When a vertex lies exactly on the boundary, the inside test may output it both as a current vertex and as an intersection. Remove consecutive duplicates before filling.

quiz.q: What is output in the outside-to-inside case for one edge?
quiz.a: The intersection point, then the current vertex.

quiz.q: Find where the edge from P = (2,5) to Q = (6,1) crosses the horizontal boundary y = 3.

beyond: Not for the exam. Graphics hardware clips in clip space before perspective division, and scissor rectangles skip whole blocks of pixels. Weiler–Atherton, Greiner–Hormann and Vatti clipping extend the idea to holes and arbitrary polygons; search those names with “polygon clipping”. Map software clips state boundaries against map polygons with the same pass-by-pass logic. Video compositing uses polygon clipping to cut a moving object from one frame and paste it into another.
